sections.heading: Remembering why I was made
sections.text: Father, you made me for your glory. If my life is not offered back to you, I am missing the reason I exist. I do not want to live as though I belong to myself, or as though my gifts, time, and choices are mainly for my own comfort. Make me a willing instrument in your hands, so that my life points back to you.
theological_themes: Human beings are created for God's glory, not self-ownership or self-exaltation.
A life disconnected from God's purpose is empty, however successful it may appear.

scripture_references.connection: God speaks of his people as those created for his glory. This grounds the prayer's confession that human life finds its meaning in belonging to God and displaying his worth.
Paul teaches that even ordinary actions are to be done for God's glory. This supports the prayer's desire that the whole life, not only religious moments, be offered to God.

sections.heading: Asking you to keep me from unbelief
sections.text: Lord, keep me from the deep sin of unbelief. If being joined to Christ is my greatest good, then pulling away from him in distrust is a terrible evil. I know I cannot cling to him perfectly in this life. My faith is weak, my obedience is unfinished, and my heart wanders. So hold me fast. Do not let me drift from Christ, and do not let me treat your command to trust him as a small thing.
theological_themes: Union with Christ is the believer's highest good and the source of spiritual life.
Unbelief is not merely weakness or uncertainty; it is a serious turning away from God's command and promise.
The believer depends on God's preserving grace because obedience and faith are imperfect in this life.

scripture_references.connection: Jesus describes abiding in him as the only way to bear fruit, because apart from him his disciples can do nothing. This directly supports the prayer's emphasis on union with Christ as essential life and fruitfulness.
This passage warns believers against an unbelieving heart that falls away and calls them to hold fast to Christ. It gives biblical weight to the prayer's plea to be kept from departing from him.

sections.heading: Receiving correction when your gifts become idols
sections.text: Father, when you take away outward comforts and blessings, teach me to listen. So often I enjoy your gifts without thanking you, use what I have without serving you, and become settled, proud, and hard. Good things can quietly become idols in my hands. They can do damage precisely because they look harmless. If a blessing is feeding my sin, take away the fuel. Love me enough to strip away whatever keeps me from loving you rightly.
theological_themes: All blessings come from God and are meant to be received with gratitude and used in his service.
Even lawful blessings can become idols when they make the heart secure apart from God.
God's fatherly discipline may remove comforts in order to expose sin and restore holiness.

scripture_references.connection: Moses warns Israel that prosperity can lead the heart to forget God and imagine that blessings came by human strength. This supports the prayer's concern that good gifts can produce pride, hardness, and practical unbelief.
God's discipline is described as fatherly and aimed at sharing his holiness. This helps frame the removal of blessings not as cruelty, but as loving correction meant to produce righteousness.

sections.heading: Choosing holiness over comfort
sections.text: Teach me to value even a small increase in holiness more than the loss of many comforts. If losing something helps me glorify you more, then let me see that as mercy, not punishment only. Make me able to say honestly that gaining more of Christ, more obedience, and more purity is better than keeping everything that makes me spiritually dull.
theological_themes: Holiness is more valuable than earthly security or comfort.
Loss can become gain when it loosens the grip of sin and makes Christ more precious.
The Christian life requires reordering loves so that God is treasured above his gifts.

scripture_references.connection: Paul counts former gains as loss because of the surpassing worth of knowing Christ. This supports the prayer's request to prize spiritual gain above outward loss.

Jesus uses severe imagery to teach that anything leading us into sin must be dealt with decisively. This illuminates the prayer's request that God remove whatever fuels sin, even if the removal is painful.

sections.heading: Wanting to love you more
sections.text: The more I truly love you, the more I see how little I love you. The more I hunger for you, the more aware I become of how weak and empty I am. The more my heart breaks over sin, the more I want it to be softened and broken still. Do not let me be satisfied with shallow love, weak desire, or casual repentance. Draw me further in.
theological_themes: Growth in grace often increases awareness of remaining sin and need.
True love for God creates a deeper desire to love him more.
Repentance is not a one-time feeling but an ongoing work of a softened heart before God.

scripture_references.connection: Jesus blesses those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, promising that God will satisfy them. This supports the prayer's longing for deeper desire and greater holiness.
David speaks of a broken and contrite heart as the kind of response God receives. This grounds the prayer's request for deeper grief over sin without implying despair.
Paul has not yet arrived, but presses on toward Christ. This fits the prayer's sense that real grace produces not complacency, but a longing for more.

sections.heading: Keeping me awake to my sin and close to Christ
sections.text: My great danger is how quickly I forget my sin. I forget the sins of my youth, and even the sins of yesterday fade from my mind by today. Search me and keep me honest. Keep me from anything that leads me toward unbelief, coldness, or losing the felt nearness of my union with Christ. Keep me close to him, trusting him, depending on him, and returning to him quickly when I stray.
theological_themes: The heart is prone to forget sin and needs God's searching and preserving grace.
Believers must be guarded from spiritual drift, unbelief, and coldness toward Christ.
The felt enjoyment of union with Christ can be weakened by sin, even though Christ remains the believer's only hope.

scripture_references.connection: The psalmist asks God to search him, expose grievous ways, and lead him in the everlasting way. This supports the prayer's plea for honesty about sin and divine keeping.
David asks to be cleansed from hidden faults and kept back from presumptuous sins. This is closely connected to the prayer's concern about forgotten sins and the need for God to restrain the heart.
John warns against denying sin and points believers to confession and God's faithful forgiveness. This supports the prayer's desire to remain awake to sin and quick to return to God.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original says that when God takes away outward blessings, it is 'for sin.' That reflects a strong providential and disciplinary reading of loss. Because Scripture does not allow every suffering or loss to be tied to a specific personal sin, the modern version frames this as fatherly correction that may expose idolatry, without making it a universal explanation for all hardship.

The phrase 'disunion from Christ by unbelief' could be read as loss of saving union. The adaptation preserves the seriousness of unbelief while expressing the prayer as a plea for preservation, closeness, and the felt enjoyment of union with Christ, rather than making a doctrinal claim about a true believer losing salvation.
significant_interpretive_choices: 'Lawful blessings are the secret idols' was rendered as good gifts quietly becoming idols, to preserve the concrete warning that morally legitimate comforts can still harden the heart.
'Remove the fuel of my sin' was kept as a direct image because it is vivid and central to the prayer's meaning: the petitioner is asking God not merely to forgive sin, but to remove what feeds it.

The repeated pattern of loving God more while grieving the lack of love was interpreted as a mark of growth in grace, not spiritual hopelessness. The modern version keeps the tension between real love and dissatisfaction with its weakness.
